newsitem.title: USA: Nasdaq to offer portfolio data on Internet site.
newsitem.headline: Nasdaq to offer portfolio data on Internet site.

text.p: The Nasdaq stock market said it plans a new portfolio tracking service on its site on the World Wide Web which can also collect data on investors for companies and member brokerage houses.

John Wall, executive vice president of market services, said the new portfolio service will be available in the next few weeks, and the market is also seeking to provide quotes from other national markets around the world.
"Investors should not only be able to see Apple's stock price here, but also how it performs overseas," he said, referring to shares computer maker Apple Computer Inc.
The site, (http://www.nasdaq.com) already includes index and most active issues data provided on a one-minute delay, plus the ability to call up 15-minute delayed price data on individual stocks.

"Where do we go from here?" John Delta, director of operations management at Nasdaq, said in a presentation at the Upside Technology Summit here. "It's content, content, content. That's what's driving our site."

The Nasdaq executives said they expect to offer financial information and data on fundamentals, such as financial results and changes in capital structure, free of charge over its Web site for 5,300 of its 5,600 stocks.

Wall said the market has "no idea" of what sort of business model it may eventually apply to the site, saying it is investing initially as a marketing tool to provide value for companies, investors and member firms.

"We're trying to get through the idea that in financial markets when you come to the Internet you go to Nasdaq," he said. Wall said he was not concerned the free information could steal business from fledgling companies offering financial data on the Web, like PC Quote and Quote.com.
"I think Quote.com is going to take it many more stages than we will...for more sophisticated professionals," he said of the financial data and research supplier.
The Nasdaq site is also capable of creating portfolios of mutual funds, the market said.

In a move that some financial industry executives said may be controversial, Wall also said the site would be capable of taking data about what portfolio an individual is keeping and distribute that information to companies and member firms.

"We're going to tell you there's no free lunch," he said, adding Nasdaq will gather data about portfolio holdings, but also individuals could enter model portfolios that would not actually reflect investments.

"I'll turn that information around and give that right back to the company," he said, noting it was difficult often for companies to identify their investors because of the use of street names for holding stock.
The information could also be fed back to brokers.
"I don't think it will be a big issue," Wall said, adding people could chose not to use the portfolio feature, and the site may contain a warning about how the data would be used.
Nasdaq said news and information was already available on the site from Businesswire and from Reuters, the worldwide news and information organisation.
Nasdaq also plans to implement Sun Microsystems Inc's Java technology for displaying scrolling quotes.
Wall said the market may also consider offering quotes in real-time, but he said it would need to address whether it could lose revenues from data vendors in the process.
Market data vendors are responsible for roughly $65-$80 million of Nasdaq's approximately $410 million in 1996 sales.
"Hopefully, we'll figure out how to make money on it as we go along," said Wall. He said investment in the Web site was "substantial," but he declined to elaborate.
